aiTutor.recap: Welcome to your first tutorial! In this lesson, we explore how applications talk to each other across the internet without sharing their private source code.

glossary.definition: Application Programming Interface: a set of predefined rules and protocols that allows different software applications to communicate.
The front-facing device or software (like your smartphone browser) that initiates a request for information.

paragraphs: Imagine walking into a restaurant. You are the customer sitting at a table, and the kitchen is the system preparing your food. You cannot simply walk into the kitchen and cook the meal yourself—there are safety, security, and privacy boundaries.
Instead, a waiter comes to your table, takes your order, delivers it accurately to the kitchen, and brings back your freshly prepared meal. In the digital world, an API is that waiter.

Whenever you check the weather on your phone, send a mobile money transfer, or view a map inside a ride-hailing app, an API takes your request to a remote server and delivers back the exact data you need.

aiTutor.explain: Think about what an API actually delivers. It does not hand over internal database passwords or raw source code; it provides an agreed-upon contract.

glossary.definition: The actual data cargo being transmitted in a network request or response (usually formatted in compact JSON).

widgetData.prompt: Complete the statement describing the fundamental role of an API:
widgetData.template: An API acts as a standardized {blank} that allows two applications to exchange data without exposing their internal databases.
widgetData.explanation: An API is a formal contract specifying valid endpoints, required inputs, and expected response formats.
widgetData.bonusFact: Over 80% of modern internet traffic consists of API calls exchanging lightweight JSON payloads.

aiTutor.explain: Consider weather or navigation apps. Ride-hailing companies don't launch their own mapping satellites; they use external APIs.

widgetData.question: When you book a ride on an app and see a live map, how does that app display Google Maps?

options.text: The app developers copied all of Google's satellite photos directly into the app file.
The app sends an API request with your coordinates to Google Maps, which returns the map tiles.
Your smartphone hardware renders satellite imagery locally without an internet connection.

widgetData.explanation: The ride-hailing app connects to Google's mapping API, requesting live map tiles on the fly.
widgetData.bonusFact: APIs allow lean startups to build complex products quickly by assembling best-in-class third-party services.

aiTutor.explain: Evaluate each statement as True or False to test your intuition about how modern APIs behave.

widgetData.instruction: Evaluate each card as True or False:

cards.statement: An API allows you to access external data without having direct access to the remote database.
cards.explanation: True! The API acts as a secure guardrail, verifying permissions before querying the database.
cards.bonusFact: Many apps you use every day, such as weather and payment apps, call APIs behind the scenes.

cards.statement: All APIs require writing Python or JavaScript code to be useful to an organization.
cards.explanation: False! No-code automation tools (like Zapier, Make, and Airtable) connect APIs visually.
cards.bonusFact: Tools like Zapier and Make let you connect two services by choosing options on screen, with no code.

cards.statement: An API response usually returns lightweight structured text (JSON) rather than a heavy full webpage.
cards.explanation: True! JSON is compact, human-readable, and saves massive bandwidth on mobile devices.
cards.bonusFact: JSON is plain text, so the same response works on any phone, browser or server.

nodes.label: 1. Request
nodes.title: HTTP Request
nodes.definition: The client sends a message containing an endpoint URL, an HTTP method (GET, POST), and optional parameters or security tokens.
nodes.bonusFact: GET requests retrieve data; POST requests send new data to be saved.

nodes.label: 2. Server Processing
nodes.title: Server Logic & Auth
nodes.definition: The API server authenticates your request, enforces rate limits, queries the internal database, and prepares the result.
nodes.bonusFact: Rate limiting protects servers from crashing if thousands of requests arrive simultaneously.

nodes.label: 3. Response
nodes.title: HTTP Response
nodes.definition: The server transmits back an HTTP status code (like 200 OK) accompanied by the requested JSON data payload.
nodes.bonusFact: If something went wrong, the response provides an error message explaining why.

widgetData.completionMessage: You've explored every step of the request-response lifecycle.
widgetData.completionBonusFact: Understanding this three-part cycle makes debugging API errors (like 404 vs 500) much faster.

aiTutor.review: Almost done! Match each standard HTTP status code with its real-world outcome to complete this tutorial.

glossary.definition: A 3-digit standardized number returned by a server indicating the outcome of a request (2xx = success, 4xx = client error, 5xx = server error).

widgetData.instruction: Match each HTTP status code with its meaning:

pairs.right: Request succeeded and data was returned
API key or user login is missing
The requested endpoint does not exist
The remote server crashed or failed internally

widgetData.explanation: Standardized status codes let developers immediately recognize whether a request succeeded (200), was blocked (401), missed (404), or broke the server (500).
